name: Captopril

fields.mechanism_of_action: Captopril is a specific competitive inhibitor of angiotensin I-converting enzyme (ACE), the enzyme responsible for the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Its beneficial effects in hypertension and heart failure appear to result primarily from suppression of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, although there is no consistent correlation between renin levels and response. By inhibiting ACE (a peptidyldipeptide carboxy hydrolase), captopril attenuates or abolishes the pressor effect of exogenously administered angiotensin I without altering pressor responses to angiotensin II or norepinephrine. ACE is identical to 'bradykininase', and captopril may also interfere with the degradation of the vasodepressor peptide bradykinin; increased concentrations of bradykinin or prostaglandin E2 may also have a role in the therapeutic effect. Inhibition of ACE results in decreased plasma angiotensin II and increased plasma renin activity (PRA) from loss of negative feedback on renin release. The reduction in angiotensin II leads to decreased aldosterone secretion, and small increases in serum potassium may occur along with sodium and fluid loss. The antihypertensive effects persist for longer than demonstrable inhibition of circulating ACE; it is not known whether vascular endothelial ACE is inhibited longer than circulating ACE. (FDA Captopril Tablets, USP label, DESCRIPTION and CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Mechanism of Action.)
indications: Hypertension: captopril tablets are indicated for the treatment of hypertension. Captopril may be used as initial therapy for patients with normal renal function; in patients with impaired renal function, particularly those with collagen vascular disease, captopril should be reserved for hypertensives who developed unacceptable side effects on other drugs or failed to respond satisfactorily to drug combinations. Captopril is effective alone and in combination with other antihypertensive agents, especially thiazide-type diuretics (the effects of captopril and thiazides are approximately additive) (FDA label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE — Hypertension; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION — Hypertension).

Congestive heart failure: captopril tablets are indicated in the treatment of congestive heart failure, usually in combination with diuretics and digitalis; the beneficial effect does not require digitalis, but most controlled clinical trial experience has been in patients receiving digitalis as well as diuretics (FDA label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE — Hypertension/Heart Failure).

Left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction: captopril tablets are indicated to improve survival following myocardial infarction in clinically stable patients with left ventricular dysfunction manifested as ejection fraction ≤ 40%, and to reduce the incidence of overt heart failure and subsequent hospitalizations for congestive heart failure in these patients (FDA label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE — Left Ventricular Dysfunction After Myocardial Infarction; supported by the SAVE study).

Diabetic nephropathy: captopril tablets are indicated for the treatment of diabetic nephropathy (proteinuria > 500 mg/day) in patients with type I insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and retinopathy; captopril decreases the rate of progression of renal insufficiency and development of serious adverse clinical outcomes (death or need for renal transplantation or dialysis) (FDA label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE — Diabetic Nephropathy).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to this product or any other angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (e.g., a patient who has experienced angioedema during therapy with any other ACE inhibitor) (FDA label, CONTRAINDICATIONS).
Do not co-administer aliskiren with captopril in patients with diabetes (FDA label, CONTRAINDICATIONS; see PRECAUTIONS, Drug Interactions — Dual Blockade of the Renin-Angiotensin System).

Contraindicated in combination with a neprilysin inhibitor (e.g., sacubitril). Do not administer captopril within 36 hours of switching to or from sacubitril/valsartan, a neprilysin inhibitor (FDA label, CONTRAINDICATIONS; see PRECAUTIONS, Drug Interactions — Neprilysin Inhibitor).
side_effects: Renal: about 1 of 100 patients developed proteinuria; renal insufficiency, renal failure, nephrotic syndrome, polyuria, oliguria and urinary frequency each reported in approximately 1 to 2 of 1,000 patients (relationship to drug use uncertain) (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Renal).
Hematologic: neutropenia/agranulocytosis has occurred; cases of anemia, thrombocytopenia and pancytopenia have been reported (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Hematologic).

Dermatologic: rash, often with pruritus and sometimes with fever, arthralgia and eosinophilia, occurred in about 4 to 7 of 100 patients (depending on renal status and dose), usually during the first four weeks; usually maculopapular, rarely urticarial, usually mild, disappearing within days of dosage reduction, short-term antihistaminic treatment and/or discontinuation, and remission may occur even if captopril is continued. Pruritus without rash occurs in about 2 of 100 patients; 7 to 10 percent of rash patients show eosinophilia and/or positive ANA titers. A reversible pemphigoid-like lesion and photosensitivity have also been reported. Flushing or pallor in 2 to 5 of 1,000 patients (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Dermatologic).

Cardiovascular: hypotension may occur (see WARNINGS and PRECAUTIONS); tachycardia, chest pain and palpitations each in approximately 1 of 100 patients; angina pectoris, myocardial infarction, Raynaud's syndrome and congestive heart failure each in 2 to 3 of 1,000 patients (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Cardiovascular).

Dysgeusia: approximately 2 to 4 of 100 patients (depending on renal status and dose) developed diminution or loss of taste perception; reversible and usually self-limited (2 to 3 months) even with continued administration; weight loss may be associated with taste loss (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Dysgeusia).

Angioedema: involving extremities, face, lips, mucous membranes, tongue, glottis or larynx in approximately 1 in 1,000 patients; angioedema involving the upper airways has caused fatal airway obstruction (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Angioedema).
Cough: reported in 0.5 to 2% of patients in clinical trials (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Cough).

Approximately 0.5 to 2 percent (not more frequent than placebo/comparators): gastric irritation, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia, constipation, aphthous ulcers, peptic ulcer, dizziness, headache, malaise, fatigue, insomnia, dry mouth, dyspnea, alopecia, paresthesias (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS).

Post-marketing by body system: anaphylactoid reactions; asthenia, gynecomastia; cardiac arrest, cerebrovascular accident/insufficiency, rhythm disturbances, orthostatic hypotension, syncope; bullous pemphigus, erythema multiforme (including Stevens-Johnson syndrome), exfoliative dermatitis; pancreatitis, glossitis, dyspepsia; anemia including aplastic and hemolytic; jaundice, hepatitis including rare cases of necrosis, cholestasis; symptomatic hyponatremia; myalgia, myasthenia; ataxia, confusion, depression, nervousness, somnolence; bronchospasm, eosinophilic pneumonitis, rhinitis; blurred vision; impotence (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — post-marketing).

An ACE-inhibitor class syndrome has been reported which may include fever, myalgia, arthralgia, interstitial nephritis, vasculitis, rash or other dermatologic manifestations, eosinophilia and elevated ESR (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS).

Altered laboratory findings: small increases in serum potassium (especially in renal impairment); hyponatremia particularly on low-sodium diets or with diuretics; transient BUN or serum creatinine elevations especially in volume/salt depletion or renovascular hypertension; positive ANA; elevations of liver transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and serum bilirubin (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Altered Laboratory Findings).

dosage.adult: Captopril should be taken one hour before meals and dosage must be individualized. Hypertension: if possible, discontinue the previous antihypertensive regimen for one week before starting captopril. Initial dose 25 mg b.i.d. or t.i.d.; if satisfactory BP reduction is not achieved after one to two weeks, increase to 50 mg b.i.d. or t.i.d. The dose usually does not exceed 50 mg t.i.d.; if BP is not controlled after one to two weeks at this dose, add a modest dose of a thiazide-type diuretic (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily). If further reduction is required, the dose may be increased to 100 mg b.i.d. or t.i.d. and then, if necessary, to 150 mg b.i.d. or t.i.d. (while continuing the diuretic). The usual dose range is 25 to 150 mg b.i.d. or t.i.d. For severe (accelerated or malignant) hypertension, captopril may be initiated at 25 mg b.i.d. or t.i.d. under close medical supervision, titrating every 24 hours or less to effect or maximum dose. Heart failure: in patients vigorously treated with diuretics who may be hyponatremic/hypovolemic, start 6.25 or 12.5 mg t.i.d. to minimize hypotension, titrating to the usual daily dosage within several days; for most patients the usual initial daily dosage is 25 mg t.i.d.; after 50 mg t.i.d. is reached, delay further increases for at least two weeks where possible to determine response; most patients improve satisfactorily at 50 or 100 mg t.i.d.; generally used in conjunction with a diuretic and digitalis, initiated under very close medical supervision. Left ventricular dysfunction after myocardial infarction: may be initiated as early as three days post-MI; after a single 6.25 mg dose, start 12.5 mg t.i.d., increase to 25 mg t.i.d. over the next several days and to a target of 50 mg t.i.d. over the next several weeks as tolerated; long-term target maintenance dose is 50 mg t.i.d. Diabetic nephropathy (type I IDDM with retinopathy and proteinuria > 500 mg/day): 25 mg t.i.d. for long-term use. (FDA label, DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION.)
dosage.maximum: A maximum daily dose of 450 mg captopril should not be exceeded (applies to hypertension and heart failure) (FDA label, DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION — Hypertension and Heart Failure).

interactions: Dual blockade of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS) with ARBs, ACE inhibitors or aliskiren is associated with increased risks of hypotension, hyperkalemia and changes in renal function (including acute renal failure) compared with monotherapy; most patients gain no additional benefit — in general, avoid combined use of RAS inhibitors. Closely monitor BP, renal function and electrolytes. Do not co-administer aliskiren in patients with diabetes; avoid aliskiren in renal impairment (GFR < 60 ml/min) (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Dual Blockade of the RAS; CONTRAINDICATIONS).
Aliskiren: contraindicated with captopril in diabetes; avoid in renal impairment (GFR < 60 ml/min) (FDA label, CONTRAINDICATIONS; PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions).

Neprilysin inhibitors (e.g., sacubitril/valsartan): contraindicated in combination; do not administer captopril within 36 hours of switching to or from sacubitril/valsartan; concomitant neprilysin inhibitors may increase angioedema risk (FDA label, CONTRAINDICATIONS; WARNINGS — Head and Neck Angioedema; PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Neprilysin Inhibitor).

mTOR inhibitors (e.g., temsirolimus, sirolimus, everolimus): co-administration with an ACE inhibitor may increase the risk of angioedema (FDA label, WARNINGS — Head and Neck Angioedema; PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions).

NSAIDs including selective COX-2 inhibitors: in elderly, volume-depleted (including diuretic-treated) or renally compromised patients, co-administration may deteriorate renal function including acute renal failure (usually reversible); monitor renal function periodically; NSAIDs may attenuate the antihypertensive effect of ACE inhibitors (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: NSAIDs including COX-2 Inhibitors).

Diuretics: patients on diuretics (especially recently instituted), severe salt restriction or dialysis may experience precipitous BP reduction usually within the first hour of the initial dose; minimize by discontinuing the diuretic or increasing salt intake ~1 week prior, or by initiating with small doses (6.25 or 12.5 mg), or provide medical supervision for at least one hour after the initial dose; thiazide-type diuretics may activate the RAS and augment captopril's effect; loop diuretics (furosemide) preferred in severe renal impairment and do not alter captopril pharmacokinetics in renally impaired hypertensive patients (FDA label, DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION; PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Hypotension — Patients on Diuretic Therapy, Agents Causing Renin Release, Loop Diuretics).

Agents having vasodilator activity (e.g., nitroglycerin, nitrates): data on concomitant use with captopril for heart failure are unavailable; if possible discontinue before starting captopril; if resumed, administer cautiously and perhaps at lower dosage (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Agents Having Vasodilator Activity).

Agents affecting sympathetic activity (e.g., ganglionic blocking agents, adrenergic neuron blocking agents): use with caution — the sympathetic nervous system may be especially important in supporting BP in patients receiving captopril alone or with diuretics. Beta-blockers add some further antihypertensive effect but the overall response is less than additive (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Agents Affecting Sympathetic Activity; CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacodynamics).

Agents increasing serum potassium (potassium-sparing diuretics such as spironolactone, triamterene, amiloride; potassium supplements; potassium-containing salt substitutes): give only for documented hypokalemia and then with caution — they may lead to a significant increase in serum potassium (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Hyperkalemia and Drug Interactions: Agents Increasing Serum Potassium).

Lithium: increased serum lithium levels and symptoms of lithium toxicity have been reported with concomitant lithium and ACE inhibitor therapy; co-administer with caution and monitor serum lithium levels frequently; a concomitant diuretic may increase the risk of lithium toxicity (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Lithium).
Cardiac glycosides: no evidence of a direct pharmacokinetic captopril–digoxin interaction in young healthy male subjects (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Cardiac Glycosides).

Allopurinol: no significant pharmacokinetic interaction in healthy volunteers after 6 days of concomitant administration; in foreign marketing experience, allopurinol used with captopril in renal failure patients has been associated with neutropenia, though this has not appeared in U.S. reports (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Allopurinol; WARNINGS — Neutropenia/Agranulocytosis).

Gold: nitritoid reactions (facial flushing, nausea, vomiting, hypotension) have been reported rarely in patients on injectable gold (sodium aurothiomalate) with concomitant ACE inhibitor therapy including captopril (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug Interactions: Gold).
Drug/laboratory test interaction: captopril may cause a false-positive urine test for acetone (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug/Laboratory Test Interaction).
fields.monitoring: Evaluation of the hypertensive or heart failure patient should always include assessment of renal function. If captopril is used in patients with impaired renal function, white blood cell and differential counts should be evaluated prior to starting treatment and at approximately two-week intervals for about three months, then periodically. In patients with collagen vascular disease or those exposed to other drugs known to affect white cells or immune response — particularly with impaired renal function — use only after a benefit/risk assessment and with caution. All patients should be told to report any signs of infection (e.g., sore throat, fever); if infection is suspected, WBC counts should be performed without delay, and upon confirmation of neutropenia (neutrophils < 1000/mm3) captopril should be withdrawn and the patient closely followed. Monitor serum potassium (hyperkalemia risk, especially with renal insufficiency, diabetes, potassium-sparing diuretics/supplements/salt substitutes), blood pressure and renal function (BUN, serum creatinine — about 20% of heart failure patients develop stable elevations >20% above normal/baseline; <5%, generally with severe preexisting renal disease, required discontinuation), and urine protein (total urinary protein > 1 g/day in ~0.7%; about one-fifth of proteinuric patients developed nephrotic syndrome). In patients on RAS inhibitors generally, closely monitor BP, renal function and electrolytes. (FDA label, WARNINGS — Neutropenia/Agranulocytosis, Hypotension; PRECAUTIONS — General: Impaired Renal Function, Hyperkalemia, Drug Interactions — Dual Blockade of the RAS; ADVERSE REACTIONS — Renal, Altered Laboratory Findings.)
fields.patient_counselling: Patients should be advised to immediately report any signs or symptoms suggesting angioedema (swelling of face, eyes, lips, tongue, larynx and extremities; difficulty in swallowing or breathing; hoarseness) and to discontinue therapy. Report promptly any indication of infection (e.g., sore throat, fever — possible neutropenia) or progressive edema (possibly related to proteinuria/nephrotic syndrome). Excessive perspiration and dehydration, vomiting or diarrhea may cause an excessive fall in blood pressure; consult the physician. Do not use potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements or potassium-containing salt substitutes without consulting the physician. Do not interrupt or discontinue medication unless instructed by the physician. Heart failure patients should be cautioned against rapid increases in physical activity. Captopril should be taken one hour before meals. Female patients of childbearing age should be told about the consequences of captopril exposure during pregnancy; discuss treatment options with women planning pregnancy and ask patients to report pregnancies as soon as possible. (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Information for Patients.)
warnings: FETAL TOXICITY (boxed warning): When pregnancy is detected, discontinue captopril tablets as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus (FDA label, BOXED WARNING; WARNINGS — Fetal Toxicity).

Fetal Toxicity (full warning): use of drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system during the second and third trimesters reduces fetal renal function and increases fetal and neonatal morbidity and death; resulting oligohydramnios can be associated with fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformations; potential neonatal adverse effects include skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure and death. When pregnancy is detected, discontinue captopril as soon as possible. In the unusual case that there is no appropriate alternative, apprise the mother of potential fetal risk and perform serial ultrasounds to assess the intra-amniotic environment; if oligohydramnios is observed, discontinue captopril unless it is considered lifesaving for the mother. Closely observe infants with in utero exposure for hypotension, oliguria and hyperkalemia (FDA label, WARNINGS — Fetal Toxicity).

Head and neck angioedema: angioedema of extremities, face, lips, mucous membranes, tongue, glottis or larynx — if involving tongue, glottis or larynx, airway obstruction may occur and be fatal; emergency therapy including subcutaneous epinephrine 1:1000 should be promptly instituted. Swelling confined to the face, mouth mucosa, lips and extremities has usually resolved with discontinuation; some cases required medical therapy. Patients co-treated with mTOR inhibitors or neprilysin inhibitors may be at increased risk (FDA label, WARNINGS — Head and Neck Angioedema).

Intestinal angioedema: reported in patients on ACE inhibitors, presenting with abdominal pain (with or without nausea/vomiting); in some cases no prior facial angioedema and normal C-1 esterase levels; diagnosed by CT/ultrasound/surgery; resolved on stopping the ACE inhibitor; include in the differential diagnosis of abdominal pain in patients on ACE inhibitors (FDA label, WARNINGS — Intestinal Angioedema).

Anaphylactoid reactions during desensitization: life-threatening reactions occurred in patients undergoing hymenoptera venom desensitization while on ACE inhibitors; reactions were avoided when ACE inhibitors were temporarily withheld and reappeared on inadvertent rechallenge (FDA label, WARNINGS — Anaphylactoid Reactions During Desensitization).

Anaphylactoid reactions during membrane exposure: reported in patients dialyzed with high-flux membranes (e.g., AN69) treated concomitantly with an ACE inhibitor, and in patients undergoing LDL apheresis with dextran sulfate absorption; consider a different dialysis membrane or a different class of medication (FDA label, WARNINGS — Anaphylactoid Reactions During Membrane Exposure; PRECAUTIONS — Hemodialysis).

Neutropenia/agranulocytosis: neutropenia (<1000/mm3) with myeloid hypoplasia has resulted; about half of neutropenic patients developed systemic or oral cavity infections or agranulocytosis features. Risk is clinical-status dependent: ~1/8,600 in normal renal function hypertension; ~1/500 in renal failure (creatinine ≥ 1.6 mg/dL); 3.7% in collagen vascular disease with impaired renal function. Usually detected within three months of starting; neutrophils typically return to normal ~2 weeks after discontinuation; ~13% of neutropenia cases ended fatally, almost all in clinically complex patients. If used in impaired renal function, obtain WBC and differential before starting and at ~two-week intervals for ~3 months, then periodically; instruct all patients to report signs of infection; on confirmation of neutropenia, withdraw captopril and follow closely (FDA label, WARNINGS — Neutropenia/Agranulocytosis).

Proteinuria: total urinary proteins > 1 g/day in about 0.7% of patients; ~90% of affected patients had prior renal disease, received relatively high doses (>150 mg/day), or both; nephrotic syndrome occurred in about one-fifth of proteinuric patients; in most cases proteinuria subsided or cleared within six months whether or not captopril was continued; BUN and creatinine seldom altered (FDA label, WARNINGS — Proteinuria).

Hypotension: excessive hypotension was rarely seen in hypertensive patients but is a possible consequence in salt/volume-depleted persons (e.g., vigorously diuretic-treated), heart failure patients, or renal dialysis patients. In heart failure, transient decreases in mean BP >20% were recorded in about half of patients, more likely after the first several doses; usually well tolerated but rarely associated with arrhythmia or conduction defects; hypotension caused discontinuation in 3.6% of heart failure patients. BECAUSE OF THE POTENTIAL FALL IN BLOOD PRESSURE IN THESE PATIENTS, THERAPY SHOULD BE STARTED UNDER VERY CLOSE MEDICAL SUPERVISION; a starting dose of 6.25 or 12.5 mg t.i.d. may minimize the hypotensive effect; follow closely for the first two weeks and whenever the captopril and/or diuretic dose is increased; reducing the diuretic dose, if feasible, may minimize the fall in BP (FDA label, WARNINGS — Hypotension).

Hepatic failure: rarely, ACE inhibitors have been associated with a syndrome starting with cholestatic jaundice and progressing to fulminant hepatic necrosis and (sometimes) death; the mechanism is not understood; patients who develop jaundice or marked elevations of hepatic enzymes should discontinue the ACE inhibitor and receive appropriate medical follow-up (FDA label, WARNINGS — Hepatic Failure).
precautions: Impaired renal function — hypertension: some patients with renal disease, particularly severe renal artery stenosis, have developed increased BUN and serum creatinine after BP reduction with captopril; dosage reduction and/or discontinuation of diuretic may be required, and in some patients it may not be possible to normalize BP and maintain adequate renal perfusion (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Impaired Renal Function).

Impaired renal function — heart failure: about 20% of patients develop stable elevations of BUN and serum creatinine >20% above normal or baseline on long-term captopril; less than 5%, generally those with severe preexisting renal disease, required discontinuation for progressively increasing creatinine (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Impaired Renal Function).

Hyperkalemia: ACE inhibitors including captopril can elevate serum potassium; at-risk patients are those with renal insufficiency, diabetes mellitus, or using potassium supplements/salt substitutes/potassium-sparing diuretics or other potassium-raising drugs. In type I diabetics with proteinuria, withdrawal for hyperkalemia was 2% (4/207); in normotensive microalbuminuric type I diabetics, none (0/116) (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Hyperkalemia).

Cough: persistent nonproductive cough has been reported with all ACE inhibitors, presumably from inhibition of bradykinin degradation; it always resolves after discontinuation; consider ACE-inhibitor cough in the differential diagnosis of cough (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Cough).

Valvular stenosis: on theoretical grounds, patients with aortic stenosis may be at particular risk of decreased coronary perfusion when treated with vasodilators because they do not develop as much afterload reduction as others (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Valvular Stenosis).

Surgery/anesthesia: captopril will block angiotensin II formation secondary to compensatory renin release in patients undergoing major surgery or during anesthesia with hypotension-producing agents; if hypotension occurs and is considered due to this mechanism, it can be corrected by volume expansion (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Surgery/Anesthesia).

Hemodialysis: hypersensitivity-like (anaphylactoid) reactions during hemodialysis with high-flux membranes (e.g., AN69) have been associated with ACE inhibitors; consider a different dialysis membrane or a different class of medication (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Hemodialysis).

In considering use of captopril, note that ACE inhibitors have less effect on BP in black patients than non-black patients, and cause a higher rate of angioedema in black than non-black patients (FDA label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE — note).

Neonates with a history of in utero exposure: if oliguria or hypotension occurs, direct attention toward support of blood pressure and renal perfusion; exchange transfusions or dialysis may be required to reverse hypotension and/or substitute for disordered renal function (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Pediatric Use).

Pediatric use: safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established; limited published experience reports weight-based dosage generally comparable to or less than adults; infants, especially newborns, may be more susceptible to adverse hemodynamic effects — excessive, prolonged and unpredictable decreases in BP and associated complications including oliguria and seizures have been reported; use in pediatric patients only if other measures for controlling blood pressure have not been effective (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Pediatric Use).
Captopril may cause a false-positive urine test for acetone (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug/Laboratory Test Interaction).
serious_adverse_reactions: Angioedema involving the upper airways (tongue, glottis, larynx) causing airway obstruction, including fatal airway obstruction (FDA label, WARNINGS — Head and Neck Angioedema; ADVERSE REACTIONS — Angioedema).
Intestinal angioedema — abdominal pain with or without nausea/vomiting, diagnosed by CT/ultrasound/surgery, resolving on discontinuation (FDA label, WARNINGS — Intestinal Angioedema).

Neutropenia/agranulocytosis — neutropenia (<1000/mm3) with myeloid hypoplasia; about half developed systemic or oral cavity infections or agranulocytosis; ~13% of neutropenia cases fatal, almost all in clinically complex patients; risk ~1/500 in renal failure and 3.7% in collagen vascular disease with impaired renal function (FDA label, WARNINGS — Neutropenia/Agranulocytosis).

Fetal injury and death — second/third-trimester exposure reduces fetal renal function, causing oligohydramnios, fetal lung hypoplasia, skeletal deformations, skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure and neonatal death (FDA label, BOXED WARNING; WARNINGS — Fetal Toxicity).

Anaphylactoid reactions — during hymenoptera venom desensitization; during hemodialysis with high-flux membranes (e.g., AN69); during LDL apheresis with dextran sulfate absorption; these can be life-threatening (FDA label, WARNINGS — Anaphylactoid Reactions During Desensitization and During Membrane Exposure).

Fulminant hepatic necrosis — rare ACE-inhibitor syndrome beginning with cholestatic jaundice and progressing to fulminant hepatic necrosis and sometimes death; patients developing jaundice or marked hepatic enzyme elevations should discontinue the ACE inhibitor (FDA label, WARNINGS — Hepatic Failure; ADVERSE REACTIONS — Hepatobiliary).
Stevens-Johnson syndrome / erythema multiforme and exfoliative dermatitis (post-marketing) (FDA label, ADVERSE REACTIONS — Dermatologic).
Nephrotic syndrome — occurred in about one-fifth of proteinuric patients (proteinuria > 1 g/day in ~0.7%) (FDA label, WARNINGS — Proteinuria; ADVERSE REACTIONS — Renal).

Hypotension with arrhythmia or conduction defects — rare instances in heart failure patients after initiation, with transient mean BP decreases >20% in about half of patients (FDA label, WARNINGS — Hypotension).
food_interactions: The presence of food in the gastrointestinal tract reduces captopril absorption by about 30 to 40 percent; captopril should therefore be given one hour before meals (FDA label, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacokinetics; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION; PRECAUTIONS — Information for Patients).

Potassium-containing salt substitutes should be used with caution because captopril decreases aldosterone production and serum potassium may rise (see interactions) (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — General: Hyperkalemia and Drug Interactions: Agents Increasing Serum Potassium).
fields.pregnancy_category: Narrative label statement (no letter category is assigned in this label): 'When pregnancy is detected, discontinue captopril tablets as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus.' (FDA label, BOXED WARNING.) The label further warns that use of drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system during the second and third trimesters reduces fetal renal function and increases fetal and neonatal morbidity and death, with resulting oligohydramnios (fetal lung hypoplasia, skeletal deformations) and potential neonatal effects of skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure and death (FDA label, WARNINGS — Fetal Toxicity). No FDA pregnancy letter category is stated in this label.
fields.pregnancy_guidance: When pregnancy is detected, discontinue captopril tablets as soon as possible. Use of drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy reduces fetal renal function and increases fetal and neonatal morbidity and death; resulting oligohydramnios can be associated with fetal lung hypoplasia and skeletal deformations; potential neonatal adverse effects include skull hypoplasia, anuria, hypotension, renal failure and death. These adverse outcomes are usually associated with use in the second and third trimester. Most epidemiologic studies examining fetal abnormalities after first-trimester antihypertensive exposure have not distinguished renin-angiotensin-system drugs from other antihypertensive agents; appropriate management of maternal hypertension during pregnancy is important to optimize outcomes for both mother and fetus. In the unusual case that there is no appropriate alternative, apprise the mother of the potential fetal risk and perform serial ultrasound examinations to assess the intra-amniotic environment; if oligohydramnios is observed, discontinue captopril unless it is considered lifesaving for the mother. Fetal testing may be appropriate based on the week of pregnancy; oligohydramnios may not appear until after the fetus has sustained irreversible injury. Patients and physicians should be aware of this. Closely observe infants with histories of in utero exposure for hypotension, oliguria and hyperkalemia. In pregnant rabbits, doses about 0.8 to 70 times (mg/kg) the maximum recommended human dose produced low incidences of craniofacial malformations; no teratogenic effects were seen in pregnant rats and hamsters at up to 625 and 150 times the maximum recommended human dose (mg/kg), respectively. Female patients of childbearing age should be told about the consequences of exposure; discuss treatment options with women planning pregnancy and ask patients to report pregnancies as soon as possible. (FDA label, BOXED WARNING; WARNINGS — Fetal Toxicity; PRECAUTIONS — Information for Patients: Pregnancy.)
fields.lactation_guidance: Concentrations of captopril in human milk are approximately one percent of those in maternal blood. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants from captopril, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or to discontinue the drug, taking into account the importance of captopril tablets to the mother. (See PRECAUTIONS — Pediatric Use: neonates with in utero exposure — exchange transfusions or dialysis may be required to reverse hypotension/disordered renal function; peritoneal dialysis is not effective for removing captopril and data on hemodialysis removal in neonates/children are inadequate.) (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Nursing Mothers and Pediatric Use.)
fields.overdose: Correction of hypotension would be of primary concern. Volume expansion with an intravenous infusion of normal saline is the treatment of choice for restoration of blood pressure. While captopril may be removed from the adult circulation by hemodialysis, there are inadequate data concerning the effectiveness of hemodialysis for removing it from the circulation of neonates or children. Peritoneal dialysis is not effective for removing captopril; there is no information concerning exchange transfusion for removing captopril from the general circulation. (FDA label, OVERDOSAGE.)
fields.pharmacokinetics: After oral administration of therapeutic doses, rapid absorption occurs with peak blood levels at about one hour. Food in the GI tract reduces absorption by about 30 to 40 percent; captopril should be given one hour before meals. Based on carbon-14 labeling, average minimal absorption is approximately 75 percent. In a 24-hour period, over 95 percent of the absorbed dose is eliminated in the urine; 40 to 50 percent is unchanged drug; most of the remainder is the disulfide dimer of captopril and the captopril-cysteine disulfide. Approximately 25 to 30 percent of circulating drug is bound to plasma proteins. The apparent elimination half-life for total radioactivity in blood is probably less than 3 hours; an accurate determination of half-life of unchanged captopril is not presently possible but is probably less than 2 hours. In patients with renal impairment, retention of captopril occurs. Pharmacodynamics: reduction of peripheral arterial resistance in hypertensive patients with either no change or an increase in cardiac output; increased renal blood flow; glomerular filtration rate usually unchanged; BP reductions usually maximal 60 to 90 minutes after an individual dose; duration of effect is dose-related; BP lowering may be progressive, so several weeks of therapy may be required for maximal effect; effects of captopril and thiazides are additive, while captopril and beta-blockers are less than additive; BP lowered to about the same extent standing and supine; orthostatic effects and tachycardia are infrequent but may occur in volume-depleted patients. Studies in rats and cats indicate captopril does not cross the blood-brain barrier to any significant extent. (FDA label, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics, Clinical studies.)
clinical_pearls: Food reduces captopril absorption by 30–40% — always dose one hour before meals; this distinguishes captopril from later ACE inhibitors that can be taken without regard to meals (FDA label, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacokinetics).

BP lowering may be progressive — several weeks of therapy may be required to achieve maximal effects; do not judge failure after 1–2 weeks without confirming titration and adherence to the pre-meal schedule (FDA label, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacodynamics; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION).

In heart failure, transient mean BP decreases >20% occur in about half of patients after the first doses; start at 6.25–12.5 mg t.i.d. in diuretic-treated/volume-depleted patients under very close medical supervision; hypotension is not per se a reason to discontinue — it is a common, desirable, self-limiting effect that stabilizes within 1–2 weeks and returns to pretreatment levels within ~2 months without loss of efficacy (FDA label, WARNINGS — Hypotension).

ACE-inhibitor cough (persistent, nonproductive) is due to bradykinin accumulation — it always resolves on discontinuation and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of cough; loss of taste (dysgeusia) is reversible and usually self-limited within 2–3 months even if drug is continued (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Cough; ADVERSE REACTIONS — Dysgeusia).

SAVE study: in clinically stable post-MI patients with LVEF ≤40%, captopril (target 50 mg t.i.d., started 3–16 days post-MI) reduced all-cause mortality by 19% (P=0.02), cardiovascular death by 21% (P=0.014), first HF hospitalizations by 22% (P=0.034), and development of overt HF by 22% (FDA label, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacodynamics: SAVE).

Diabetic nephropathy: in type I IDDM with retinopathy and proteinuria ≥500 mg/day, captopril 25 mg t.i.d. reduced risk of doubling of serum creatinine by 51% and the combined endpoint of ESRD or death by 51% (P<0.01), and reduced proteinuria by 30% within 3 months (FDA label, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacodynamics; DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION — Diabetic Nephropathy).

Neutropenia risk is highest in renal failure and collagen vascular disease (3.7%) — check WBC before starting and at two-week intervals for three months, then periodically; counsel every patient to report sore throat or fever (FDA label, WARNINGS — Neutropenia/Agranulocytosis).
Captopril may cause a false-positive urine test for acetone — interpret urine acetone results with caution in diabetics (FDA label, PRECAUTIONS — Drug/Laboratory Test Interaction).

The antihypertensive effect is less in black patients than non-black patients, and angioedema is more frequent in black patients — factor this into drug selection and counselling (FDA label, INDICATIONS AND USAGE).
Abrupt withdrawal has not been associated with rebound hypertension (FDA label, CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacodynamics).
brand_names: Captopril Tablets, USP — no proprietary brand name is stated on this label; distributed by Hikma Pharmaceuticals USA Inc. (Berkeley Heights, NJ); manufactured by Hikma Pharmaceuticals, Amman, Jordan. The original US innovator brand Capoten is not named in this generic label and its current US availability is not stated here.
black_box_warnings: WARNING: FETAL TOXICITY — When pregnancy is detected, discontinue captopril tablets as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus. See WARNINGS: Fetal Toxicity. (FDA label, BOXED WARNING — exact wording.)
fields.renal_dose_adjustment: Because captopril is excreted primarily by the kidneys, excretion rates are reduced in patients with impaired renal function; these patients take longer to reach steady-state and reach higher steady-state levels for a given daily dose, and may respond to smaller or less frequent doses. For patients with significant renal impairment, the initial daily dosage should be reduced and smaller increments used for titration, which should be quite slow (one- to two-week intervals). After the desired therapeutic effect is achieved, the dose should be slowly back-titrated to determine the minimal effective dose. When concomitant diuretic therapy is required, a loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide), rather than a thiazide diuretic, is preferred in patients with severe renal impairment. The label gives no specific creatinine-clearance cutoff for captopril. (FDA label, DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION — Dosage Adjustment in Renal Impairment; CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY — Pharmacokinetics: retention in renal impairment.)
fields.administration_instructions: Captopril tablets should be taken one hour before meals; dosage must be individualized. Take on an empty stomach — food reduces absorption by about 30 to 40 percent. Available as 12.5 mg (white, round, debossed 'W-7', scored), 25 mg (white, round, debossed 'WW 172', quadrisect scored), 50 mg (white, oblong, debossed 'WW 173', scored) and 100 mg (white, oblong, debossed 'WW 174', scored) tablets. Store at 20–25°C (68–77°F), keep bottles tightly closed and protect from moisture; dispense in a tight, light-resistant container with a child-resistant closure. If a dose is missed, the label gives no specific missed-dose instruction — do not double doses without prescriber advice. (FDA label, DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION; DESCRIPTION; HOW SUPPLIED.)
